message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how you can launch a Google Compute Engine instance that has an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (or the closest equivalent that Google currently offers) and runs Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.

> ⚠️ **Important note** – Google Cloud does **not** offer the RTX A6000 directly.  
> The closest match in the current GPU catalog is the **NVIDIA A100** (PCI‑e or SXM) or the **Tesla T4** if you only need a lower‑tier GPU.  
> If you absolutely need an RTX A6000, you’ll have to use a custom image or a third‑party marketplace image that contains the driver stack, but the underlying hardware will still be one of the GPUs listed above.

---

## 1. Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# 1️⃣  Set your project and zone
PROJECT_ID="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-a"

# 2️⃣  Pick a machine type that supports GPUs
#    e.g., n1-standard-8 (8 vCPUs, 30 GB RAM)
MACHINE_TYPE="n1-standard-8"

# 3️⃣  Choose the GPU type
#     - RTX A6000 is not available; use A100 PCI‑e instead
GPU_TYPE="nvidia-tesla-a100"
GPU_COUNT=1

# 4️⃣  Pick the OS image
IMAGE_PROJECT="ubuntu-os-cloud"
IMAGE_FAMILY="ubuntu-2004-lts"

# 5️⃣  Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create my-rtx-instance \
  --project=${PROJECT_ID} \
  --zone=${ZONE} \
  --machine-type=${MACHINE_TYPE} \
  --accelerator=type=${GPU_TYPE},count=${GPU_COUNT} \
  --image-project=${IMAGE_PROJECT} \
  --image-family=${IMAGE_FAMILY} \
  --boot-disk-size=200GB \
  --boot-disk-type=pd-ssd \
  --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE \
  --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
  --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh   # optional: install drivers, CUDA, etc.
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU + RAM configuration that supports GPUs |
| `--accelerator` | Adds the GPU(s) to the VM |
| `--image-project` / `--image-family` | Base OS image (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS) |
| `--boot-disk-size` | Size of the boot disk |
| `--boot-disk-type` | SSD for better I/O performance |
| `--maintenance-policy` | Keeps the VM running during host maintenance |
| `--scopes` | Grants full Cloud Platform access (needed for GPU driver installation) |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script` | Optional script that installs NVIDIA drivers & CUDA after boot |

> 👉 **Tip:** If you want to automatically install the latest NVIDIA driver and CUDA toolkit, create a `startup.sh` script that runs `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-525 cuda-toolkit-11-8` (adjust versions as needed).

---

## 2. Using the REST API (JSON)

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine API directly (e.g., from a CI/CD pipeline or a custom application), here’s the exact JSON payload you would POST to:

```http
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/instances
Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "my-rtx-instance",
  "machineType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 200,
        "diskType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100"
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\napt-get update\napt-get install -y nvidia-driver-525 cuda-toolkit-11-8"
      }
    ]
  },
  "scheduling": {
    "preemptible": false,
    "onHostMaintenance": "MIGRATE",
    "automaticRestart": true
  }
}
```

### How to obtain the access token

```bash
gcloud auth application-default print-access-token
```

Replace `{PROJECT_ID}` and `{ZONE}` with your actual values. The `acceleratorType` field uses the same naming convention as the `gcloud` CLI (`nvidia-tesla-a100`). If you want a different GPU, change the type accordingly (e.g., `nvidia-tesla-p4`, `nvidia-tesla-v100`, etc.).

---

## 3. Quick sanity check

After the instance boots, SSH into it and verify the GPU:

```bash
ssh my-rtx-instance@<EXTERNAL_IP>
nvidia-smi
```

You should see the NVIDIA A100 (or whichever GPU you selected) listed, along with the driver version and CUDA toolkit.

---

## 4. Summary

| Step | Command | What it does |
|------|---------|--------------|
| 1 | `gcloud compute instances create ...` | Creates a VM with the specified GPU and OS |
| 2 | `POST /instances` (REST) | Same as above, but via HTTP |
| 3 | `nvidia-smi` | Confirms the GPU is visible inside the VM |

Feel free to tweak the machine type, disk size, or GPU count to fit your workload. Happy computing!
